name: David Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work lates at a car parts distribution centre, two till half ten. Garages order brake discs, filters, exhausts in the morning and want them by the next day, so we pick and pack all evening. I've got a wrist scanner and a route on the screen, and I'm usually on the heavy aisle with discs and batteries.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the parts. My dad runs a two-bay garage in our town, so I grew up handing him spanners, and I can tell a Ford disc from a Vauxhall one by the weight. What wears me out is the late finish, and the batteries, which are heavy and awkward. I use AI every day, mostly to research shares and to sort my dad's invoices, which he hates doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, though I'd be a bit surprised. I use it every day, and it's already better than that. But if it stalls, the warehouse carries on as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype merchants got it wrong, and that hard work still beats clever talk. I'd probably post that in the car forum I'm on, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine either way. I've got about nine months saved and some shares, and I own half a van with my cousin. In this picture I keep the job, keep investing and keep helping Dad at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the lates and keep putting 400 a month into shares. I'd do more Saturday work at Dad's garage, maybe start doing his parts ordering properly with AI so he stops over-buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, because I like change, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the van with your cousin for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekend jobs, house moves and collecting parts for Dad's customers. It brings in maybe 300 a month each. It's not a business yet, it's more of a habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you look up to, work-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, honestly. My dad has worked for himself for 30 years and never taken a penny he didn't earn. I'd like my own name over a door one day.

say: The **hype merchants** got it wrong, and hard work still beats clever talk.
I'd post that, **half joking**, on the car forum I use.
think: I'd be **fine** either way, with nine months saved and some shares.
I'd keep the job and spend **weekends** at Dad's garage.
do: Keep putting **400 a month** into shares.
Do Dad's **parts ordering** with AI so he stops over-buying.
Keep the **weekend van** jobs with his cousin.
feel: **Calm**, if a bit flat, because he likes change.
S0.quote: My dad has worked for himself for 30 years and never taken a penny he didn't earn. I'd like my own name over a door one day.
fieldNote: He uses AI **daily** but still frames success as hard work.
His **dad's garage** is the centre of his future plans.
He already has a **side income** with his cousin's van.

steps.text: Keep working lates on the car parts heavy aisle
Keep weekend removal and parts runs in the van with his cousin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like what I expect. The ordering, the invoices, the customer emails, AI does all that. At work, robots creep in for the light stuff like filters before they ever handle a battery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should stop moaning and learn the tools, because that's what's paying. I'd say it on the forum and at the canteen, and I'd get some stick for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this is good for me. My picking job lasts a good few years because the heavy aisle is hard to automate. Cheap thinking AI means my dad's two-bay garage can run like a big one without paying an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set Dad up with an AI system for bookings, invoices and parts this year. I'd go to four lates a week and do one weekday at the garage learning diagnostics. I'd put another 2,000 into shares in the robot and AI firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly a bit excited. I can see where I fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your dad go along with AI running his bookings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd moan for a month and then love it. Last year I set up his online diary and now he shows it to customers like he invented it. He just needs someone he trusts to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office lads at our site, the ones who handle returns claims from garages. AI does that in a weekend. I'd tell them to get a forklift licence, but most of them wouldn't listen.

say: People should stop moaning and **learn the tools**, because that's what pays.
I'd say it on the forum and **take some stick** for it.
think: The **heavy aisle** is hard to automate, so my job lasts years.
Cheap thinking AI lets **Dad's garage** run like a big one.
do: Set up an **AI system** for bookings, invoices and parts at Dad's garage.
Drop to **four lates** and spend one weekday learning diagnostics.
Put another **2,000 into shares** in robot and AI firms.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, because he can see where he fits.
S1.quote: Cheap thinking AI means my dad's two-bay garage can run like a big one without paying an office.
fieldNote: He sees the change as **good for him** and his family business.
His worry is for the **office lads** handling returns claims.
He would **bet money** on the firms doing the automating.

steps.text: Set up AI bookings, invoices and parts ordering at Dad's garage
Spend one weekday a week learning diagnostics at the garage
Put another 2,000 into robot and AI company shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's fast. AGI in 2028 means the garage paperwork and diagnostics brains are free. Then 2031, robots that can pick batteries, and maybe even change brake pads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to be bold, not to sit and wait for a government scheme. Families that pull together and own something will come through it. I'd say that even though I know it's easy for me to say with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose the warehouse job by 2031, no question. And the garage only lasts if robot mechanics are expensive for a while, which I think they would be, at first. I've got three years of hands-on work left that's truly mine, and a few more in the garage if I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd hand in my notice at the warehouse and go full-time with Dad, using my savings to cover the pay drop. I'd sell some shares to buy a proper diagnostic kit and get the garage booked solid with AI. I'd want to be the garage that buys the first repair robot in 2031, not the one it puts out of business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like a challenge, but this is a lot of money and a lot of family riding on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's everything. The thinking AI makes a small garage cheaper to run straight away, and I get three years of full bookings before the robots catch up. If I use those years well, we can afford the robot instead of being beaten by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it goes wrong and the garage fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm 31 with nothing but a trade and my savings half gone. That's the bit that keeps me up. But there are plenty of warehouses here, at least until 2031, so I could always go back for a bit.

say: This is the moment to **be bold**, not to wait for a government scheme.
Families that **pull together** and own something will come through it.
think: I'd **lose the warehouse job** by 2031, no question.
The garage lasts only while **robot mechanics** stay expensive.
do: Quit the warehouse and go **full-time** at Dad's garage in the first month.
Sell some shares to buy a **diagnostic kit** and fill bookings with AI.
Plan to buy the **first repair robot** around 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, because a lot of money and family ride on him.
S2.quote: I'd want to be the garage that buys the first repair robot in 2031, not the one it puts out of business.
fieldNote: He'd **move first**, quitting rather than waiting to be pushed.
His bet is that the **three-year gap** pays for a robot later.
He admits the **failure case** is what keeps him up.

steps.text: Hand in notice at the car parts warehouse in the first month
Join Dad's two-bay garage full-time as a mechanic
Sell some shares to buy a garage diagnostic kit
Run the garage bookings and invoices with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, so AGI by 2031 and robots by 2034. That's the same as the fast one, just with time to do it in order instead of all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plan now and don't expect anyone to save you. And I'd say it's a good time for apprenticeships, because the people who can fix things will be wanted for longer than the people who write emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at the warehouse a couple of years and bank the wage. Then move to the garage full-time before 2031, once Dad's ready to step back a bit. I'd still expect the picking job to go, but on my timetable, not theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, four lates a week, one weekday at the garage, the AI bookings system for Dad, and a part-time course in electric car repair. I'd keep 400 a month into shares. I'd also look at buying the unit next door to the garage if it comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be busy, a bit tired, but it would feel like it's mine to win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electric car repair, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half the cars coming into my dad's garage will be electric by then, and Dad won't touch them. Somebody in our family needs the ticket for high-voltage work. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your dad about these plans straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bits of them. He's proud, he doesn't like being told his garage needs saving. I'd show him the numbers from the AI bookings first, and then talk about the rest over a Sunday dinner.

say: **Plan now** and don't expect anyone to save you.
It's a good time for **apprenticeships**, because fixers will be wanted longer.
think: I'd **bank the wage** at the warehouse for a couple of years first.
The picking job still goes, but on **my timetable**, not theirs.
do: Work **four lates** and one weekday at the garage in year one.
Take a part-time course in **electric car repair**.
Look at buying the **unit next door** to the garage.
feel: **Uneasy** and busy, but it feels like it's his to win.
S3.quote: Half the cars coming into my dad's garage will be electric by then, and Dad won't touch them. Somebody in our family needs the ticket for high-voltage work.
fieldNote: Five years lets him leave the warehouse **in order**, not in a rush.
He spots a **gap** his father won't fill: electric cars.
He'd handle his proud dad with **numbers first**, then Sunday dinner.

steps.text: Keep four late shifts a week at the warehouse for two years
Take a part-time course in electric car repair
Price up buying the unit next door to the garage
Set Dad's garage up with AI bookings and invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, AGI by 2036, robots by 2039. I'd be 37 when the AI lands. That's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift, and anyone my age who wastes it has only themselves to blame. Learn a trade, own a share of something, and look after your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one is good for me. By 2039 I'd want to own the garage with Dad, maybe two sites, and be the one buying the robots. The warehouse would be a memory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd stay at the warehouse full-time and save hard, maybe 1,000 a month into the garage fund. I'd do the electric car course and start doing Dad's diagnostics on Saturdays. I'd marry my girlfriend Anya, which we've been talking about, because the future wouldn't feel so rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy and focused, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Anya. Does she see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend Anya is a primary school teacher, so she thinks her job is safer than mine. She's probably right, because kids need a person. Between her wage and my plans, we'd be steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that could still go badly for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If big chains with robots open everywhere and undercut small garages. That's the real risk, not the robots themselves. So the plan is to be good enough that people want us, not just cheap.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, and anyone who wastes it has themselves to blame.
Learn a trade, **own a share** of something, and look after your family.
think: By 2039 I'd want to **own the garage** with Dad, maybe two sites.
The warehouse job would be gone, but it would be **a memory**, not a loss.
do: Save **1,000 a month** into a garage fund while still at the warehouse.
Do the **electric car course** and Saturday diagnostics at the garage.
S4.quote: My girlfriend Anya is a primary school teacher, so she thinks her job is safer than mine. She's probably right, because kids need a person.
fieldNote: With ten years he sees this picture as **good for him**.
His partner's **teaching job** gives the household ballast.
He names **big chains**, not robots, as the real threat.

steps.text: Save 1,000 a month into a fund for the garage
Complete the electric car repair course
Buy into Dad's garage as a part-owner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to bet my savings and Dad's garage on getting the timing right. What would help is cheap loans for small family firms to buy their own robots, instead of only the big chains getting them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who ends up owning the robots. That's the whole question for me. If small family firms own the robots, we're fine. If only the giants own them, we're all just pickers again.

headlineQuote: If small family firms own the robots, we're fine. If only the giants own them, we're all just pickers again.
portrait: David is a 27-year-old picker on the **heavy aisle** of a car parts warehouse.
He uses AI daily, invests in **shares**, and runs a weekend van with his cousin.
His future lies in his dad's **two-bay garage**, which he wants to modernise.
In the fast AGI picture he'd **quit first** and bet his savings on the garage.
With more time he'd train in **electric car repair** and aim to own robots, not compete with them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to bet his savings and Dad's garage on **timing**.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small family firms to buy their own robots, not only big chains.
